source: The expansion, the cosmic microwave background and the amounts of hydrogen and helium all point to a hot, dense early universe.
Students picture the Big Bang as an explosion at one point in an empty space.

The age of the universe comes from running the expansion backward. Going back, everything was closer together, denser and hotter, until about 13.8 billion years ago the universe was extremely hot and dense. That is the Big Bang theory: not an explosion at a point, but the expansion and cooling of space from that hot, dense state. Three separate lines of evidence support it.

Stretching space stretches light: a wavelength grows in proportion to the size of the universe, $1 + z = \frac{\text{size now}}{\text{size then}}$. By Wien's law, a longer peak wavelength means a lower temperature, so the radiation's temperature falls as the universe grows: $T = T_{\text{now}}(1 + z)$. The CMB came from redshift about 1100, when the temperature was $2.725 \times 1101 \approx 3000$ K, just when hydrogen atoms could form. A hot, dense past predicts this glow everywhere, with exactly a blackbody's shape, and that is what satellites (COBE, WMAP, Planck) measured.

The Big Bang is the expansion and cooling of the universe from a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. Evidence: the expansion, the cosmic microwave background at $2.725$ K, and the amounts of hydrogen and helium.
The cosmic microwave background: a blackbody at $2.725$ K, peaking near $1$ mm (log scales).
Where does a $2.725$ K blackbody peak? Use $\lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{6}\ \text{nm·K}}{T}$.
Millimeter waves are microwaves, hence the name.
How hot was the background radiation at redshift $z = 1100$?
At that temperature hydrogen nuclei can just hold on to their electrons, so the universe turned transparent.

It is natural to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off at one spot in empty space, with galaxies flying out from there. The evidence says space itself expanded everywhere at once. There is no center, and the CMB arrives evenly from every direction because every part of space was part of the hot early universe. Check: if galaxies flew out from one point, we could find the point; Hubble's law looks the same from every galaxy.
